items.title: EEG study reports altered cortical oscillations and connectivity in tinnitus patients versus controls
items.whyMatters: This is mechanism research, not a treatment test: it looks for brain-activity patterns that accompany tinnitus and the emotional distress it causes. Such markers could one day help target neuromodulation or measure it objectively, but this study does not show that any treatment works.
items.summary: A cross-sectional resting-state EEG study from Tianjin University applying spectral parameterization (aperiodic exponent, alpha center frequency) plus source-level phase-locking connectivity to tinnitus patients versus healthy controls, reporting a higher aperiodic exponent, slowed temporal alpha peak frequency, and altered auditory–parietal/ACC–prefrontal connectivity said to relate to tinnitus-related emotional distress. The aperiodic/periodic decomposition framing is a relatively fresh methodological angle on long-described tinnitus EEG abnormalities. none reported (abstract gives only directional 'significantly higher/reduced' statements without effect sizes, p-values, or N)

detail.population: Patients with subjective tinnitus and healthy controls (age range, hearing status, tinnitus duration, and distress stratification not reported in the abstract)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Group differences in resting-state EEG measures: aperiodic exponent, alpha center frequency, and source-level phase-locking value connectivity between tinnitus patients and healthy controls
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Relationship of EEG features to tinnitus-related emotional distress; comparison of findings against patterns previously described in primary depressive disorder
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational EEG group-comparison study with no treatment and no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating outcome reported.
detail.distressOutcome: none — distress was used only as a correlate/framing for EEG features; no intervention was delivered and no distress questionnaire change was measured.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported (non-interventional EEG recording; no safety outcomes described)
limitations: Sample size not reported in the abstract; likely small single-centre cohort
Cross-sectional case-control design — cannot establish causality or direction between EEG features and distress
No treatment arm, no randomization, no blinding — provides no efficacy information
Distress measurement instrument (THI/TFI/anxiety scales) not specified in the abstract
Hearing loss is a major confounder of auditory-cortex EEG measures and no matching/control for audiometric thresholds is described
Source-level connectivity from scalp EEG is sensitive to inverse-solution and volume-conduction assumptions; multiple-comparison handling not reported
No independent replication; aperiodic exponent findings in tinnitus remain inconsistent across labs
Claim of specificity versus depression is not supported by a depression comparison group
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships; academic (Tianjin University / Haihe Laboratory) affiliations, no manufacturer involvement stated. Funding source not reported in the abstract.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Uncontrolled study of intratympanic dexamethasone reports questionnaire improvement in 65 tinnitus patients
items.whyMatters: Steroid injections through the eardrum are still widely offered for tinnitus, but this study had no comparison group, so the improvement in questionnaire scores could easily reflect the placebo effect or natural fluctuation rather than the drug. It does not change the current assessment that intratympanic injections lack convincing evidence for tinnitus.
items.summary: A small single-arm observational study from two Indian centres reporting THI improvement after four weekly intratympanic dexamethasone injections in 65 patients with severe disabling tinnitus. Nothing methodologically new — it repeats the uncontrolled design that has characterised intratympanic steroid reports for two decades, and the authors themselves state it cannot establish efficacy. THI category distribution before vs after: mild 21.5% → 67.7%; moderate 63.1% → 32.3%; severe 15.4% → 0% (P < .05). No mean THI scores, no change scores, no confidence intervals and no responder definition reported.

detail.population: 65 patients aged 18-60 with tinnitus of at least 1 month duration described as severe/disabling, reported as associated with sensorineural hearing loss in the methods but 'with or without' SNHL in the title/conclusion; 60% male, majority under 30 years; single Indian department (Navodaya Medical College), Oct 2019–Sep 2021
detail.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) severity category after 4 weekly intratympanic dexamethasone injections (4 mg/mL, 0.4–0.6 mL), assessed at completion of treatment
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported (complications noted qualitatively)
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed; THI is a distress/handicap questionnaire and says nothing about the loudness of the percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI category shifts were measured only within-group with no control arm, no blinding and no follow-up beyond the end of injections, so natural history, regression to the mean and placebo/procedural expectancy cannot be separated from any drug effect.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported — no audiometric, sleep, or quality-of-life outcomes are given despite SNHL being an inclusion criterion.
detail.safety: 'Minimal complications were noted' after 4 weekly injections in 65 patients — no enumeration of tympanic membrane perforation, vertigo, otalgia, infection or hearing change, and no defined adverse-event collection period is described.
limitations: Single-arm descriptive design with no control or sham arm — authors explicitly concede this
No randomization and no blinding of patients or assessors
Only questionnaire (THI) outcome; no loudness matching, no audiometry results, no TFI
Results presented only as severity-category percentages, no mean change, SD, CI or responder rate
Outcomes assessed at end of the 4-week injection course only — no durability follow-up
Inconsistency between methods (all patients had SNHL) and title/conclusion ('with or without SNHL')
Unusual demographic (majority under 30) raises questions about case selection and generalisability
Retrospective/descriptive data collection 2019–2021 published 2026; no registry number or funding statement reported
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflict of interest; no funding source or manufacturer involvement stated (dexamethasone is a generic drug). Absence of a funding statement is itself a reporting gap.
detail.source: The journal of international advanced otology
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small feasibility trial: sound-paired non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation found safe, but no effect on tinnitus loudness or TFI
items.whyMatters: A 30-person trial tested pairing electrical stimulation of the vagus nerve with a sound matched to the patient's own tinnitus; it was safe and practical to deliver, but tinnitus loudness and the standard tinnitus questionnaire did not improve more than in the placebo group. Hints of reduced unpleasantness, anxiety and better sleep in one small group are preliminary and need a properly powered trial before they mean anything.
items.summary: First randomized safety/feasibility trial of noninvasive vagus nerve stimulation paired with a replica of the patient's own tinnitus sound (a Pavlovian 'reconditioning' rationale), compared with simultaneous pairing and with randomly-timed (placebo) pairing. The novelty is the delayed/parasympathetic pairing schedule rather than any demonstrated efficacy. none reported in the abstract (no effect sizes, means or p-values given); reported as 'no significant differences between groups' for tinnitus loudness change and TFI change, with significant reductions in unpleasantness, anxiety and PSQI in the delayed-AS group described by the authors as exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons

detail.population: Adults with chronic, pure-tone (tonal) tinnitus, Dunedin, New Zealand
detail.primaryEndpoint: Safety and feasibility of paired noninvasive VNS + tinnitus-matched auditory stimulation over nine sessions in three weeks
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Tinnitus loudness ratings, Tinnitus Functional Index, tinnitus unpleasantness, anxiety, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, EEG activity/functional connectivity; assessed at baseline, post-treatment and one-month follow-up
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — there was no significant between-group difference in tinnitus loudness ratings, and with 10 participants per arm the trial could not have detected a modest loudness effect either way.
detail.distressOutcome: limited — the TFI, the validated distress measure, showed no between-group difference; the reported gains in unpleasantness and anxiety were in one arm only, exploratory, and not corrected for multiple comparisons.
detail.otherOutcomes: Sleep: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index improved in the delayed auditory-stimulation arm (exploratory, uncorrected). EEG: changes reported in regions associated with tinnitus and unpleasant-sound processing; mechanistic, not a clinical outcome. Hearing outcomes not reported.
detail.safety: No serious adverse events were reported across 30 participants receiving nine sessions over three weeks, with follow-up to one month; the abstract does not enumerate minor or expected adverse events (e.g. ear discomfort, skin irritation, headache).
limitations: Very small sample (n=10 per arm); explicitly a safety/feasibility trial, not powered for efficacy
Primary endpoint was safety/feasibility — all clinical outcomes are secondary or exploratory
Positive findings (unpleasantness, anxiety, PSQI) were uncorrected for multiple comparisons and confined to a single arm
Blinding procedures and success of blinding not described in the record
Short intervention (nine sessions/three weeks) and short follow-up (one month)
No numerical effect sizes or confidence intervals available in the abstract
Claimed parasympathetic activation from noninvasive VNS was not verified, as the authors acknowledge
Single centre, single research group; no independent replication
detail.funding: independent — academic trial (University of Otago); one author reports equipment/supplies provided by Delft University of Technology (an academic institution, not a commercial device manufacturer); remaining authors declare no competing interests. Note senior author D. De Ridder has a long-standing research program in tinnitus neuromodulation, which is a non-financial intellectual interest.
detail.source: Neuromodulation : journal of the International Neuromodulation Society
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Popping sound and streaming water-like tinnitus in Cochlin-tomoprotein-confirmed perilymphatic fistula with antecedent barotrauma.
items.whyMatters: For people whose tinnitus started after diving, flying, straining or a blast, the specific sound they hear — a popping noise or a running-water sound — may be a hint that fluid is leaking from the inner ear, a condition that can sometimes be repaired surgically. This is a diagnostic clue from a retrospective review, not evidence that any tinnitus treatment works.
items.summary: A large multicenter Japanese retrospective series links specific tinnitus/aural percept qualities — a 'popping sound' after external barotrauma and 'streaming water-like' tinnitus after internal pressure-related barotrauma — to biochemically confirmed (Cochlin-tomoprotein-positive) perilymphatic fistula, and reports that absence of a fistula sign does not exclude PLF. This is diagnostic-phenotype work, not treatment evidence. Category 2: CTP positivity 60% with popping sound vs 12% without (OR 10.88; 95% CI 1.63–68.66; p = 0.035). Category 3: streaming water-like tinnitus 41% vs 16% (OR 3.75; 95% CI 1.30–10.31; p = 0.019); nystagmus 30% vs 12% (OR 3.12; 95% CI 1.18–8.70; p = 0.033). Fistula sign: not associated.

detail.population: Patients with antecedent barotrauma (category 2 = external barotrauma, category 3 = internal pressure-related) drawn from 736 patients who underwent Cochlin-tomoprotein (CTP) testing at 80 Japanese institutions; retrospective multicenter sample
detail.sampleSize: 149 barotrauma cases analyzed (from a 736-patient CTP-tested pool)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Association between clinical features (popping sound, streaming water-like tinnitus, nystagmus, fistula sign) and CTP-confirmed perilymphatic fistula status
detail.secondaryEndpoints: CTP positivity rates by barotrauma category (17% category 2; 22% category 3)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no treatment was tested and no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed; the paper concerns the qualitative character of the percept as a diagnostic clue, not its loudness.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life outcomes were measured.
detail.otherOutcomes: Vestibular sign (nystagmus) associated with CTP positivity in internal barotrauma; fistula sign unhelpful for ruling out PLF. No hearing outcome data reported in the abstract record.
detail.safety: Not reported — retrospective diagnostic study with no intervention and no adverse-event reporting described.
limitations: Retrospective chart-based design with no prospective protocol
Symptom descriptions ('popping sound', 'streaming water-like tinnitus') are subjective, non-standardized and recorded by many different clinicians across 80 sites
Exploratory analyses explicitly not adjusted for multiple comparisons; several p-values near 0.05
Very wide confidence intervals indicate small subgroup cell counts
Selection bias: only patients already suspected enough to receive CTP testing were included, inflating apparent diagnostic value
No treatment, no follow-up, no tinnitus-specific outcome instruments
Institutional patent/royalty interest in the CTP ELISA index test
detail.funding: unclear-to-conflicted: Saitama Medical University (the authors' institution) holds the patent for the CTP ELISA test and receives royalties via a licensing/technical-support relationship with Biomedical Laboratories. Authors state this did not influence findings, but the study promotes clinical use of the institution's own patented test and this should be flagged.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Review proposes the auditory striatum as a circuit link between sound filtering, decision-making and tinnitus
items.whyMatters: Researchers argue that a part of the brain's basal ganglia that filters sounds and turns them into decisions may be involved in tinnitus. This is a theory paper built mostly on animal studies — it does not test or support any treatment.
items.summary: A narrative review synthesizing circuit-level (largely animal) work on the auditory striatum — its role in sensory gating, temporal processing and auditory-guided decision-making — and proposing that disrupted sensory weighting/selection in this region may contribute to tinnitus. No new data, no patients, no treatment.

detail.population: Not reported — narrative review of circuit-level neuroscience literature, predominantly animal work
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported (narrative review, no prespecified endpoint)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the review reports no psychoacoustic loudness matching or percept measurements in humans; the tinnitus link is a hypothesis about circuit function, not an outcome.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or any patient-reported distress outcome is involved.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported
limitations: Narrative review, not systematic — no search strategy, inclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessment
Evidence base is largely rodent circuit neuroscience; human tinnitus relevance is inferred, not demonstrated
Tinnitus is a brief speculative extension of the main argument rather than the review's core subject
No patient data, no outcomes, no treatment tested
Funding and COI statements not available in the provided record
detail.funding: unclear — no funding or competing-interest statement is available in the supplied record; authors are academic (Peking University Third Hospital, Peking University, Renji Hospital) with no apparent device or drug manufacturer involvement
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Brain imaging study reports altered spontaneous activity patterns in chronic tinnitus, linked to neurotransmitter maps
items.whyMatters: This study compared brain scans of 80 people with long-term tinnitus to 68 without it and found differences in resting brain activity in hearing and attention-related regions, which the authors linked statistically to maps of serotonin, dopamine, glutamate and GABA systems. It is basic mechanism research — it tested no treatment and says nothing about whether any therapy reduces tinnitus loudness or distress.
items.summary: A cross-sectional resting-state fMRI study (80 chronic tinnitus patients vs 68 healthy controls) combining static and dynamic ALFF with spatial correlation against PET/SPECT-derived neurotransmitter atlases, reporting increased sALFF in left superior temporal gyrus, decreased dALFF in right precuneus, and spatial coupling of these alterations with serotonin transporter, dopaminergic, glutamatergic, GABAergic and VAChT maps. The dynamic (time-varying) component plus neurotransmitter-map coupling is the incremental novelty; abnormal auditory/precuneus spontaneous activity in tinnitus is already well documented. Increased sALFF in left superior temporal gyrus and decreased dALFF in right precuneus in tinnitus vs controls (GRF correction, voxel P<0.001, cluster P<0.05). No effect sizes, correlation coefficients, or clinical scale values reported in the abstract.

detail.population: Adults with chronic subjective tinnitus and healthy controls at a single Chinese hospital (Henan Provincial People's Hospital); tinnitus duration, hearing status, laterality and distress severity not reported in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: Between-group differences in static and dynamic amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (sALFF, dALFF) on resting-state fMRI
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Spatial correlation of ALFF alteration maps with normative neurotransmitter receptor/transporter distribution maps
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational imaging study with no treatment and no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness ratings reported.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other distress outcomes reported in the abstract, and no intervention was tested.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported (non-interventional MRI study)
limitations: Cross-sectional observational design — cannot establish causality or direction (tinnitus vs hearing loss vs comorbid anxiety/depression)
Single centre, modest sample, no independent replication cohort
Neurotransmitter 'coupling' is a spatial correlation with group-average PET/SPECT atlases from other populations, not individual neurochemical measurement
Hearing-loss matching, tinnitus duration/laterality, and distress severity not reported in the abstract; audiometric confounding is a major known issue in tinnitus fMRI
No clinical outcomes, no treatment arm, no follow-up
ALFF findings in tinnitus have been inconsistent across prior studies; risk of analytic flexibility and false positives despite GRF correction
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing interests; no manufacturer involvement apparent. Funding source not stated in the record.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Review article summarizes the links between tinnitus and cognitive function
items.whyMatters: Many people with tinnitus report trouble concentrating, more distractibility and mental fatigue, and this review pulls together the brain-network explanations researchers use for that. It contains no new data and tests no treatment, so it does not change what is known to work.
items.summary: Nothing substantively new: a German-language narrative review from the Charité Tinnitus Center summarizing existing hypotheses about how tinnitus relates to attention, working memory and executive control via frontoparietal/default-mode network changes and limbic involvement. It offers a conceptual argument for multidimensional, interdisciplinary care rather than any new data.

detail.population: Not reported — narrative review of prior literature; authors explicitly state no new human or animal studies were conducted
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported (no prespecified endpoint; narrative review)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the review reports no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness ratings and tests no intervention; its claim that therapy should reduce 'tinnitus perception' is an aspiration, not a measured loudness outcome.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no distress instrument (THI/TFI/TQ) outcomes are reported; emotional stress is discussed only as a mechanistic mediator of cognitive load.
detail.otherOutcomes: Discusses cognitive domains (attention, working memory, executive control, distractibility, mental fatigue) as correlates of tinnitus, and notes some studies find tinnitus's negative cognitive impact exceeds that of accompanying hearing loss or depression/anxiety — but without pooled effect sizes or a systematic search.
detail.safety: Not reported
limitations: Narrative review with no stated search strategy, inclusion criteria, or risk-of-bias assessment
No new data; authors state no studies on humans or animals were conducted for this article
No quantitative synthesis or effect sizes
German-language, online ahead of print; full text not reviewed beyond abstract
Cross-sectional associations between tinnitus and cognition cannot establish causal direction (hearing loss, age, depression, sleep and medication are strong confounders)
Therapeutic recommendations (multidimensional/interdisciplinary care) are expert opinion, not derived from trial evidence in this paper
detail.funding: independent — all six authors declare no conflict of interest; no funding source stated. Note the group (Charité Tinnitus Center, Mazurek et al.) is an active tinnitus research and treatment center whose own multidisciplinary care model is favored by the review's conclusion.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Donepezil failed to beat placebo for chronic tinnitus in a small double-blind trial
items.whyMatters: Donepezil, a drug used in dementia, was tested for tinnitus for the first time in a placebo-controlled trial and did not work better than placebo on tinnitus severity or on measurements of the sound itself. Negative results like this are useful because they help rule out repurposed drugs and discourage off-label prescribing based on theory alone.
items.summary: First randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of donepezil (an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor) in chronic subjective tinnitus; it found no statistically significant benefit over placebo on any instrument, including psychoacoustic measures, with only post-hoc confidence-interval 'trends' favoring the drug. No statistically significant between-group differences on any instrument; confidence-interval analysis of responders achieving ≥7-point and ≥11-point THI improvement 'suggested a potential clinically meaningful trend favoring donepezil'; complete tinnitus remission in 1 patient, in the donepezil arm. No effect sizes, p-values or means reported in the abstract.

detail.population: Adults with chronic subjective, non-somatosensory tinnitus at a single Brazilian academic ENT center (FMUSP), plus an age- and gender-matched comparison group; the abstract's description of the two groups vs. the drug/placebo randomization is ambiguous
detail.sampleSize: 35 per group as stated in the abstract (exact number randomized to donepezil vs placebo not clearly reported)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not clearly specified; stated as symptom improvement assessed by the evaluation instruments (THI appears to be the principal tinnitus outcome)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Tinnitus VAS, psychoacoustic tinnitus measurements (pitch/loudness matching), cognitive measures (CDR, MMSE)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — psychoacoustic tinnitus measurements were performed and showed no significant difference from placebo; the single reported remission is an anecdote, not a loudness finding.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI and VAS showed no statistically significant separation from placebo; the ≥7/≥11-point THI responder 'trend' is a post-hoc confidence-interval observation and must not be presented as a distress benefit.
detail.otherOutcomes: Cognitive screening (MMSE, CDR) collected; no significant between-group differences reported. Authors mention a possible greater benefit among participants using hearing amplification — an unplanned subgroup observation only. Sleep and quality-of-life outcomes not reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — the abstract gives no adverse-event data despite donepezil's known cholinergic side-effect profile (nausea, diarrhea, bradycardia, insomnia); full-text review needed.
limitations: Small sample (≈35 per group), underpowered for modest effects
Primary endpoint not explicitly defined in the abstract; multiple instruments raise selective-reporting risk
Positive framing rests on post-hoc confidence-interval/responder analyses and an unplanned amplification subgroup
Single anecdotal remission highlighted despite a null primary result
No effect sizes, p-values, or dispersion reported in the abstract
Adverse events not reported
Single center, 3-month treatment, no post-treatment follow-up described
Group structure (tinnitus group vs matched control group vs drug/placebo allocation) ambiguous as described
Funding source not identified
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing interests and state funders had no role in design, writing or publication decision; the funding source itself is not named in the abstract (academic institutional support presumed, unverified).
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Survey of Korean university hospitals shows tinnitus care is broader than in 2013, but new therapies remain rarely used
items.whyMatters: This is a snapshot of what tinnitus specialists in Korea actually do, not a test of whether any treatment works. It shows that despite more psychological assessment and more hearing-based rehabilitation, drugs and retraining therapy still dominate and newer options like CBT programmes, apps and neuromodulation are seldom used routinely.
items.summary: A 2025 nationwide cross-sectional survey of tinnitus practice patterns among otologists at Korean university hospitals, benchmarked descriptively against a comparable 2013 survey. It documents shifts toward broader classification, psychological assessment and structured questionnaires, expanded auditory rehabilitation (CROS/BiCROS, cochlear implantation), and only limited routine uptake of CBT-based, digital, and neuromodulation therapies. 34 respondents from 28/45 university hospitals (62% of hospitals represented); no formal hypothesis testing performed because individual-level 2013 data were unavailable; no effect sizes or outcome numbers reported

detail.population: Otologists registered with the Tinnitus Study Group of the Korean Otologic Society, practising at Korean university hospitals (clinicians, not patients)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Self-reported practice patterns: tinnitus classification, diagnostic work-up, treatment strategies, hearing-aid fitting practice, and perceived barriers
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Descriptive item-level comparison with the 2013 nationwide survey; perceived barriers to care (lack of effective treatments, online misinformation, unrealistic patient expectations, reimbursement limits)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is a clinician practice survey with no patient outcome data; it says nothing about the loudness of the tinnitus percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other distress outcomes were measured; increased use of psychological assessment is a practice pattern, not a distress benefit.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported (no patient-level sleep, QoL or hearing outcomes)
detail.safety: Not reported — no patient safety data collected; the survey notes frequent intratympanic steroid use as an evidence-practice gap but reports no adverse-event information.
limitations: Cross-sectional clinician self-report survey — no patient outcomes of any kind
Very small sample (34 respondents) and incomplete institutional coverage (28 of 45 hospitals); non-response bias likely
Respondents drawn from a tinnitus special-interest group, so practice is probably more specialised than average Korean ENT care
No formal statistical comparison with 2013; individual-level 2013 data unavailable and several items not directly comparable
Findings are specific to Korean university hospitals and reimbursement environment; limited generalisability
Only abstract-level detail available (online ahead of print); item-level numbers not verifiable here
detail.funding: unclear — funding and COI statements are not present in the available record; no manufacturer involvement is apparent from the academic affiliations (Inje, Ewha Womans, Yonsei universities)
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Review article revisits the auditory thalamus (medial geniculate body) as a gateway in tinnitus
items.whyMatters: Researchers continue to explore how a relay station in the brain's hearing pathway may fail to filter out signals after hearing loss, which is one leading explanation for why tinnitus arises. This is background theory only — it tests no treatment and changes nothing about current options.
items.summary: Nothing substantively new: this is a Chinese-language narrative review summarising how the medial geniculate body (auditory thalamus) gates, filters and integrates auditory signals, and how disrupted gating plus central gain changes after hearing loss may contribute to tinnitus perception. It restates an established thalamic gating / central gain framework rather than reporting new data.

detail.population: Not reported — narrative review of anatomy/physiology literature, no human or animal cohort of its own
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — no outcomes; review of mechanisms
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or percept ratings were performed; the paper only discusses hypothesised thalamic mechanisms of tinnitus perception.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or any distress, anxiety or sleep outcome was measured.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported
limitations: Narrative (non-systematic) review — no search strategy, no inclusion criteria, no risk-of-bias assessment
No original data, no participants, no outcomes
Short article (5 pages) in a specialty Chinese-language journal; full text and reference base not available in English for verification
Mechanistic speculation about thalamic gating and central gain is not tied to any measured tinnitus outcome
Cannot be used to support or refute any treatment
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest (所有作者声明无利益冲突); no funding or manufacturer involvement stated
detail.source: Zhonghua er bi yan hou tou jing wai ke za zhi = Chinese journal of otorhinolaryngology head and neck surgery
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Industry survey on willingness to accept a brain implant for tinnitus completes with 1,000 respondents; no results posted
items.whyMatters: A company developing an implanted brain stimulator for severe tinnitus has finished asking 1,000 patients how much surgical risk and cost they would accept — this tells us about patient attitudes and the company's product plans, not about whether any treatment works. No tinnitus outcomes were measured, so nothing here shows any effect on loudness or distress.
items.summary: ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT06782308 flipped to COMPLETED (primary completion and completion 2026-09-03) with 1,000 actual respondents — a Neurosoft Bioelectronics patient-preference questionnaire on whether people with chronic tinnitus would accept a surgically implanted closed-loop brain stimulator, and what they would pay. No results, no publication, and no clinical outcomes of any kind are posted. none reported — only enrollment (1,000 actual) and completion date (2026-09-03) are posted

detail.population: Adults (18+) with self-reported or clinician-diagnosed chronic (≥3 months), burdensome subjective tinnitus, recruited as a non-probability online sample
detail.primaryEndpoint: Acceptance of invasive neuromodulation (surgically placed brain implant) and its surgical risks for chronic tinnitus, summarized as acceptance rates, stratified by reported tinnitus characteristics including annoyance and loudness
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Usability preferences for implantable neuromodulation systems; willingness and ability to pay (USD range)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an attitudes/preferences questionnaire with no intervention and no psychoacoustic measurement; loudness is only used as a self-reported stratifier.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other distress outcome was measured as an endpoint; no treatment was delivered.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported — a questionnaire with no intervention; no adverse event data collected or posted.
limitations: Not a treatment study: survey of stated preferences, no intervention, no control, no randomization
No results posted and no peer-reviewed publication; only the registry status change is verifiable
Non-probability (self-selected online) sample — high risk of selection bias toward severely affected and treatment-seeking patients
Hypothetical willingness-to-accept-risk and willingness-to-pay questions are known to overstate real-world uptake
Sponsor is the device developer and the sponsor-investigator is a company employee; survey instrument not published
No IPD sharing; no DMC; no independent oversight
detail.funding: manufacturer-funded — lead sponsor/responsible party is Nicolas Gninenko, Clinical Neuroscientist at Neurosoft Bioelectronics SA, which is explicitly developing the implantable tinnitus device the survey is designed to support; survey links to the company's product page.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: New US registry study will track hyperbaric oxygen outcomes across 41 conditions, including tinnitus — no results before 2035
items.whyMatters: A Dartmouth-led registry plans to record how patients fare after hyperbaric oxygen treatment for a long list of conditions, with tinnitus among them. It has no comparison group and no tinnitus-specific questionnaire, so it will not be able to show whether HBOT actually helps tinnitus — and it has not started collecting data.
items.summary: A new ClinicalTrials.gov registration (NCT07240649, Dartmouth-Hitchcock, investigator-sponsored) for a single-arm Phase 4 multicenter registry of hyperbaric oxygen for 41 'emerging indications', one of which is tinnitus; status updated 2026-09-09 to NOT_YET_RECRUITING with an estimated start of November 2026 and completion in 2035. No results, no tinnitus-specific outcome measure, and no control group. none reported (study not yet recruiting; primary completion estimated 2035)

detail.population: Patients receiving clinical HBOT at participating centers for any of 41 'emerging' indications (including tinnitus, post-COVID condition, inflammatory bowel disease, osteonecrosis, retinal occlusions, wounds); tinnitus-specific eligibility criteria and expected tinnitus subgroup size are not stated
detail.sampleSize: 100 estimated total across all 41 indications combined (tinnitus subgroup size not reported)
detail.primaryEndpoint: EuroQol EQ-5D-5L quality-of-life score (0-1 index plus 0-100 VAS), measured within one week before starting and within one week of finishing HBOT
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Condition-specific instruments (Urogenital Distress Inventory, bowel symptom questionnaire, head/neck questionnaire, perianal Crohn's index, HOOS, Strauss wound score, calciphylaxis/frostbite/pyoderma packages) plus a 4-level subjective global assessment; no tinnitus-specific instrument (no THI, TFI, TQ, or loudness match) appears in the visible record
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating is planned, and no data exist; this record says nothing about the tinnitus percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no validated tinnitus distress instrument (THI/TFI/TQ) is listed and no data have been collected.
detail.otherOutcomes: Generic quality of life (EQ-5D-5L) is the only planned outcome applicable to tinnitus patients; sleep and hearing are not assessed.
detail.safety: Not reported — no participants enrolled; the record notes no Data Monitoring Committee (oversightHasDmc: false).
limitations: No data yet — study is NOT_YET_RECRUITING with estimated start Nov 2026 and completion Dec 2035
Single-arm, unrandomized, unblinded, no sham or control group; pre-post design highly vulnerable to placebo, regression to the mean and natural fluctuation, which is a major issue in tinnitus
Basket design spanning 41 heterogeneous indications with only 100 total participants estimated — the tinnitus subgroup will be tiny and uninterpretable
Primary endpoint is generic EQ-5D-5L quality of life; no tinnitus-specific distress instrument and no loudness measurement
No DMC; registry data collection across centers with differing practice patterns
Tinnitus aetiology (acute vs chronic, SSNHL-related vs idiopathic) not specified in the visible record
detail.funding: Unclear — investigator-initiated (Jay C. Buckey Jr., Dartmouth-Hitchcock, with Dartmouth College); no industry sponsor listed, but funding source and any hyperbaric-industry ties are not disclosed in the registry record, and registry projects run by hyperbaric medicine centers have an inherent interest in expanding HBOT indications.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: VA randomized trial of notched-noise therapy for tinnitus completes enrollment of 108; results not yet posted
items.whyMatters: A federally funded, independent randomized trial has finished testing whether 'notched' noise delivered through hearing aids reduces tinnitus, compared with plain white noise or amplification alone. Until the results are published, it changes nothing — but it is one of the few sound-therapy trials that measured the loudness of the tinnitus itself, not just how much it bothers people.
items.summary: Registry update only: the VA's notched-noise therapy RCT (NCT04661995) has moved to COMPLETED status with 108 participants actually enrolled and a final completion date of 31 May 2026. No results, publication, or effect sizes have been posted.

detail.population: US Veterans with chronic tinnitus (device-fitted with ear-level combination instruments; those needing amplification continued hearing aid use during the washout)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Change in Tinnitus Functional Index (TFI) from baseline at 4, 8 and 12 weeks
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Psychoacoustic tinnitus loudness and pitch matching; auditory evoked potential (AEP) and EEG measures (per the detailed description; full secondary outcome list truncated in the retrieved record)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no outcome data are posted; the trial does prespecify psychoacoustic loudness matching alongside TFI, so when results appear it is one of the few sound-therapy trials able to speak to the percept itself rather than only distress.
detail.distressOutcome: none — the TFI primary endpoint is unreported; nothing here supports any distress claim.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse event data posted; registry lists no data monitoring committee (oversightHasDmc: false).
limitations: No results posted — status change only; efficacy remains unknown
Participant-only blinding (single mask); outcome assessors/audiologists fitting devices not blinded, which matters for psychoacoustic matching and TFI administration
The 'placebo comparator' (amplification-only) is an active treatment, not a sham, so a null result could reflect equal benefit rather than no benefit
Short 8-week intervention with only 4 weeks of post-treatment follow-up
Single-site VA Veteran population limits generalizability (predominantly male, noise-exposed, high TBI/PTSD comorbidity)
Psychoacoustic loudness matching has known poor test-retest reliability
detail.funding: independent — VA Office of Research and Development (CDA-2 career development award, NIH/RR&D ID 1IK2RX003281-01A2); no industry sponsor listed, though commercial streaming hearing aids are used and any device/manufacturer support is not disclosed in the record.
detail.source: VA Office of Research and Development
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small Turkish trial comparing group CBT, breathing exercises and psychoeducation for tinnitus distress now listed as completed; no results yet
items.whyMatters: This registry entry only tells us a small 70-person study has finished, not what it found. If results are published, it may add a little detail on how group CBT compares with simple relaxation breathing for tinnitus-related distress — but it will not tell us anything about whether tinnitus gets quieter.
items.summary: A registry status update: this small Turkish three-arm randomized study (CBT vs 4-7-8 breathing exercise vs single-session psychoeducation, n=70) is now marked COMPLETED, with actual primary completion 2026-06-02 and full completion 2026-06-15. No results have been posted, so nothing new is known about outcomes.

detail.population: Adults 18-65 with subjective tinnitus, no hearing loss, no hearing-aid use, no current DSM-5 psychiatric disorder; single Turkish centre (Ankara Etlik City Hospital, Ege University sponsor)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI) at baseline, week 7 post-intervention, 1 month and 6 months — a DISTRESS/handicap measure, not loudness
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Beck Anxiety Inventory and Beck Depression Inventory at the same four timepoints
detail.comparisonType: between-group — but no data posted, so no comparison can be reported yet; within-group change must never be presented as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the trial measures no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating whatsoever; THI and Beck scales say nothing about the loudness of the percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — THI, BAI and BDI are the distress endpoints, but no outcome data have been posted, so no distress effect can be credited.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported (no sleep, QoL, or audiometric outcome measures listed)
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse event outcome measures listed; the record notes a data monitoring committee exists and the interventions are not FDA-regulated drugs or devices.
limitations: No results posted — status change only
Small sample (n=70, ~23 per arm) for a three-arm comparison
No masking of participants or (as recorded) assessors; self-reported primary outcome is highly susceptible to expectancy

Unequal contact time (seven 90-minute group sessions vs twice-daily home breathing vs a single psychoeducation session) confounds intervention effect with attention/contact — acknowledged by investigators
No inert/waitlist control; psychoeducation arm is a weak comparator, so the design can support relative but not absolute efficacy claims
Investigators state an explicit directional hypothesis favouring CBT in an unblinded trial (bias risk)
Registered prospectively only in part: first submitted 2026-06-01, essentially at primary completion
Single centre, narrow population (no hearing loss, no psychiatric comorbidity) limits generalisability
Individual participant data will not be shared publicly
Described by investigators as exploratory
detail.funding: independent — academic sponsor (Ege University) with a public hospital collaborator; no industry funding or device/drug manufacturer involvement disclosed in the record
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: US survey analysis links combined work and leisure noise exposure, and hearing difficulty, to tinnitus-related trouble falling asleep
items.whyMatters: In a large national US survey, people with tinnitus who had both workplace and recreational noise exposure — and especially those with hearing difficulty — were more likely to say tinnitus made it hard to fall asleep. It is a snapshot of associations, not proof that noise causes the sleep problem, and it does not test any treatment.
items.summary: A survey-weighted cross-sectional analysis of the 2014 NHIS hearing supplement quantifying how combined occupational plus leisure noise exposure and hearing difficulty relate to tinnitus-related trouble falling asleep in a nationally representative U.S. sample. It is epidemiological association work, not treatment evidence. Weighted 12-month tinnitus prevalence 11.5%; 41.8% of those with tinnitus reported trouble falling asleep. Combined occupational + leisure noise: aOR 1.69 (95% CI 1.30–2.19, P<0.001); leisure only: aOR 1.37 (1.03–1.84, P=0.033); occupational only: aOR 1.13 (0.92–1.39, P=0.23); P-for-trend <0.001. Hearing difficulty: aOR 1.78 (1.47–2.15, P<0.001).

detail.population: U.S. adults aged ≥18 years from the 2014 National Health Interview Survey; primary outcome analysed among the subset reporting tinnitus in the past 12 months
detail.sampleSize: 36,697 adults total; n = 4,292 with tinnitus for the primary outcome; n = 33,507 for the secondary short-sleep analysis
detail.primaryEndpoint: Self-reported tinnitus-related trouble falling asleep among adults with tinnitus
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Short sleep duration in the full sample (reported as '>7 hours' in the abstract, which appears to be a typographical error for <7 hours)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating was performed; the study measures only self-reported sleep disturbance attributed to tinnitus.
detail.distressOutcome: none — this is an observational correlate analysis with no intervention and no validated distress instrument (no THI/TFI/TQ); it describes who is more likely to report tinnitus-related sleep trouble, not any change in distress.
detail.otherOutcomes: Sleep: 41.8% of tinnitus respondents reported trouble falling asleep attributed to tinnitus; a secondary short-sleep-duration analysis was conducted in the full sample but no effect sizes for it are given in the abstract.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational survey analysis with no intervention.
limitations: Cross-sectional design: no causal inference and no temporal ordering between noise exposure, hearing difficulty and sleep trouble
All exposures and outcomes are self-reported; no audiometry, no psychoacoustic tinnitus measurement, no validated tinnitus or insomnia questionnaire
Data are from 2014, over a decade old, analysed and published in 2026
Attribution of sleep trouble to tinnitus is respondent-assigned and vulnerable to recall and attribution bias
Secondary short-sleep endpoint described inconsistently ('>7 hours'), suggesting reporting error
Residual confounding (e.g. mental health, medication, shift work, comorbid insomnia) not addressed
Author group is predominantly computing/engineering and general medicine with no listed tinnitus or audiology expertise; funding and COI not stated in the available record
detail.funding: unclear — no funding statement or COI disclosure in the available record; no manufacturer involvement is apparent since no product or treatment is evaluated.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Large German population study: hearing loss linked to memory and brain changes, tinnitus alone is not
items.whyMatters: In 4,400 adults, people reporting hearing loss had slightly worse memory and brain-scan findings associated with dementia risk, but people reporting tinnitus without that pattern showed no such differences. It says nothing about whether any tinnitus treatment works, and because tinnitus was recorded only as present/absent it cannot rule out effects in people with severe tinnitus.
items.summary: In a large general-population German cohort (SHIP-TREND) with cognitive testing and structural MRI, self-reported hearing loss was associated with worse verbal memory and dementia-relevant brain changes (partly mediated by white matter hypointensity volume), whereas self-reported tinnitus alone showed no association with cognition or adverse brain structure despite being strongly correlated with hearing loss (OR 7.5). Self-reported hearing loss associated with tinnitus: OR 7.5 (95% CI 6.0 to 9.3; p < 0.001). White matter hypointensity volume partially mediated 8.8% of the association between self-reported hearing loss and immediate recall. Hearing loss associated with worse memory and unfavourable brain measures along the central auditory pathway and AD-implicated regions; tinnitus alone not associated with cognition or brain measures, and no relevant combined effects. Effect sizes for individual associations not given in the abstract.

detail.population: Community-dwelling adults aged 20-84 years from northeastern Germany (SHIP-TREND baseline); 1,455 reported hearing loss (679 clinically relevant degree), 874 reported tinnitus
detail.sampleSize: 4,420 participants analysed (4,400 completed hearing self-assessment, 3,937 tinnitus self-assessment, 2,144 with T1-weighted MRI)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Associations of self-reported hearing loss and tinnitus with cognitive performance (verbal memory, executive function) and with global/regional brain volumes and cortical thickness on T1-weighted MRI, adjusted for age, sex and further dementia risk factors
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Mediation analyses (e.g. white matter hypointensity volume as mediator); combined effects of hearing loss plus tinnitus; association between hearing loss and tinnitus
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational epidemiological study with no treatment and no psychoacoustic loudness measurement; tinnitus was captured only by self-report of presence.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or other distress instrument was reported, and no intervention was tested.
detail.otherOutcomes: Hearing: self-reported hearing loss in 1,455 (679 clinically relevant) and strong co-occurrence with tinnitus. Cognition: worse verbal memory (immediate recall) with hearing loss. Brain structure: lower volumes/cortical thickness along central auditory pathway and in AD-relevant regions with hearing loss; white matter hypointensities suggesting a cerebrovascular link.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational study with no intervention; no adverse-event assessment applicable.
limitations: Cross-sectional design at baseline only — no causal inference and no longitudinal cognitive trajectory
Hearing loss and tinnitus both self-reported; no audiometry, no tinnitus characterisation (loudness, pitch, duration, distress severity)
Tinnitus exposure is a crude binary presence variable, so severe/distressing tinnitus cannot be separated from mild intermittent tinnitus — a null result may mask effects in severe cases
MRI available in only about half the sample (2,144/4,420), raising selection concerns
Residual confounding despite adjustment (education, cardiovascular, hearing-aid use not clarified in abstract)
Single regional cohort (northeastern Germany), limiting generalisability
Multiple regional brain measures tested; correction for multiplicity not stated in the abstract
detail.funding: independent — academic population cohort (University Medicine Greifswald/DZNE) with no device or drug manufacturer involvement in the tinnitus question; two senior authors declare unrelated pharma honoraria/personal fees (HJG: Neuraxpharm, Servier, Idorsia, Janssen Cilag; AF: Lilly, Biogen, Eisai), disclosed as outside the submitted work.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Small study finds subtle auditory nerve signal differences in people with tinnitus and normal hearing tests
items.whyMatters: It adds to evidence that 'normal hearing' tinnitus may involve damage too subtle for a standard hearing test to detect, which could eventually help explain where tinnitus comes from. It tests no treatment and changes nothing about what patients should do today.
items.summary: A cross-sectional case-control ABR study reporting that middle-aged adults with tinnitus and normal audiograms/DPOAEs show selective wave I abnormalities (reduced amplitude at low intensity; prolonged latency in chronic tinnitus) plus suprathreshold changes (steeper wave V latency-intensity slope, higher V/I ratio) that differ by tinnitus duration. The chronicity-dependent stratification (acute <6 months vs chronic ≥6 months) is the main novel element; cochlear-synaptopathy-style ABR findings in tinnitus with normal hearing are themselves a long-contested literature. Pure-tone thresholds, wave V thresholds and DPOAEs did not differ across groups. Chronic tinnitus: prolonged wave I latency at 55, 75 and 80 dB nHL; steeper wave V latency-intensity slope; higher V/I ratio at 80 dB nHL. Both acute and chronic tinnitus: reduced wave I amplitude at 45 dB nHL. Interpeak latencies and wave V ABR growth ratio showed no robust group differences. No effect sizes, confidence intervals or exact p-values are given in the abstract.

detail.population: Middle-aged adults with tinnitus and clinically normal audiograms and preserved DPOAEs, subdivided into acute (<6 months) and chronic (≥6 months) tinnitus, compared with healthy normal-hearing controls; single centre in Suzhou, China
detail.sampleSize: 74 tinnitus patients (101 ears) and 15 controls (30 ears)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Click-evoked ABR measures (absolute wave latencies/amplitudes, interpeak latencies, intensity-response slopes, wave V/I amplitude ratio, wave V growth ratio) across 45–90 dB nHL compared between tinnitus subgroups and controls
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Pure-tone thresholds, wave V thresholds and DPOAE measures across groups
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is a mechanistic/physiological study with no treatment and no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness ratings reported.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ or any distress, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life outcome is reported.
detail.otherOutcomes: Hearing measures (pure-tone thresholds, wave V thresholds, DPOAEs) were equivalent across groups, supporting that the ABR differences are not explained by conventional threshold or outer-hair-cell differences.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational ABR/DPOAE testing only, no intervention administered.
limitations: Cross-sectional observational design; cannot establish whether ABR changes cause tinnitus or follow it
Very small and unbalanced control group (15 participants / 30 ears) versus 74 patients, limiting power and precision for between-group contrasts
Ear-level analysis (101 vs 30 ears) risks inflating apparent sample size despite mixed-effects modelling

Acute vs chronic groups compared cross-sectionally rather than longitudinally, so 'chronicity-dependent' changes may reflect cohort differences (e.g., age, noise history, aetiology) rather than progression
Click ABR wave I amplitude is highly variable and sensitive to electrode montage, sex, head size and noise history; abstract reports no effect sizes or confidence intervals
Multiple comparisons across many ABR metrics and 10 intensity levels with findings appearing at scattered intensities (55, 75, 80 dB but not others), raising concern about selective/chance positives
Single-centre, single-population (Chinese middle-aged adults); no independent replication
No tinnitus loudness matching, psychoacoustic characterisation or questionnaire outcomes reported, so findings cannot be linked to percept severity
Extended high-frequency audiometry status not stated in the abstract, a common confounder in 'normal audiogram' tinnitus studies
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing financial interests or personal relationships; academic hospital/university affiliations, no manufacturer involvement disclosed. Funding source not stated in the abstract.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Narrative review outlines surgical and endovascular options for pulsatile tinnitus from sigmoid sinus wall anomalies
items.whyMatters: For the small subset of people whose pulsatile tinnitus comes from a bulge or thin spot in a large vein near the ear, surgery or stenting can sometimes remove the actual sound source. This review is a clinicians' decision guide rather than new evidence, and the authors themselves say good long-term outcome studies are still missing.
items.summary: A narrative review from a Korean academic group summarizing diagnosis and transmastoid surgical options (resurfacing, re-roofing, diverticulectomy with multilayer reconstruction) for pulsatile tinnitus from sigmoid sinus wall anomalies, and proposing a stepwise algorithm for choosing conservative vs. surgical vs. endovascular management. It contributes an expert decision framework and material-selection discussion, but no new patient data. none reported (abstract states only that 'in carefully selected patients, these strategies can achieve high rates of PT improvement' without figures)

detail.population: Not reported — narrative review; no defined patient cohort, discussion of patients with venous-type pulsatile tinnitus due to sigmoid sinus diverticulum or dehiscence
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — narrative review with no prespecified endpoint
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Not reported
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — the review reports no new psychoacoustic or loudness-matching data; claims of 'PT improvement' are narrative summaries of prior case series, not new measurement of the percept.
detail.distressOutcome: none — 'meaningful gains in quality of life' is asserted narratively with no THI/TFI or QoL instrument data presented here.
detail.otherOutcomes: Discusses reconstructive materials (polymethylmethacrylate cement, hydroxyapatite, autologous bone) and acknowledges uncertainty about long-term durability; also discusses differential diagnosis (dural AVF, high-riding jugular bulb, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) and when stenting or systemic therapy should be preferred.
detail.safety: Not reported — the review discusses patient selection, contraindications and 'red flags' where transmastoid surgery may be ineffective or carry substantial risk, but reports no new adverse-event data.
limitations: Narrative review, not systematic: no search strategy, inclusion criteria, risk-of-bias assessment, or pooled analysis
No new patient data, no numbers, no control groups
Underlying literature is dominated by small single-arm retrospective series with placebo-prone subjective outcomes
Proposed algorithm is expert opinion, not validated
Authors themselves note the absence of prospective studies with long-term follow-up
Online-ahead-of-print; full text not reviewed beyond abstract
detail.funding: independent — authors (Seoul National University Bundang Hospital, Chungbuk National University, SNU College of Medicine) declare no conflicts of interest; no funding source stated in the record. Note that a surgical review by active surgeons carries inherent procedural-advocacy bias even absent financial COI.
detail.source: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association : JCMA
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Large Iranian population study finds chronic headache linked to higher odds of tinnitus
items.whyMatters: In a survey of over 10,000 adults, people with chronic headaches were about 1.8 times more likely to report tinnitus, adding to evidence that the two conditions often travel together. This is an association only — it does not show that headaches cause tinnitus or that treating one will help the other.
items.summary: A large population-based cross-sectional analysis (Hoveyzeh Cohort, n=10,009) in southwestern Iran reporting a 10.5% self-reported tinnitus prevalence and an independent association between ICHD-3-defined chronic headache and tinnitus (adjusted OR 1.81). It adds regional epidemiological data from an under-studied Arab population, but is not treatment evidence. Tinnitus prevalence 10.5%; chronic headache prevalence 7.5%. Chronic headache associated with tinnitus OR = 1.81 (95% CI 1.48-2.22). Other predictors: older age OR = 2.23; dizziness OR = 1.90; head trauma OR = 1.76; male sex OR = 0.77; higher physical activity OR = 0.69.

detail.population: Adults aged 35-70 years in an Arab community in Hoveyzeh, Khuzestan, southwestern Iran (baseline data from the Hoveyzeh Cohort Study)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Association between chronic headache (ICHD-3 classified) and self-reported tinnitus, via multivariable logistic regression
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Prevalence of tinnitus and chronic headache; other independent predictors of tinnitus (age, dizziness, head trauma, sex, physical activity)
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational prevalence/association study with no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating of the tinnitus percept; tinnitus was captured only as a self-reported yes/no.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI, TFI, TQ, anxiety, sleep or quality-of-life instruments were administered or reported.
detail.otherOutcomes: Reports co-occurrence of dizziness and head trauma as independent predictors of tinnitus; no hearing thresholds, sleep or QoL outcomes reported in the abstract.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational study with no intervention.
limitations: Cross-sectional design: cannot establish temporality or causation between chronic headache and tinnitus
Tinnitus ascertained by self-report only, with no audiometric confirmation, loudness matching, or severity/handicap instrument
No characterization of tinnitus subtype (pulsatile vs non-pulsatile, somatic, unilateral) which matters for the headache link
Single region, restricted age band (35-70) and one ethnic community — limited generalizability
Potential residual confounding (hearing loss, noise exposure, analgesic use, medication ototoxicity, depression/anxiety) not clearly accounted for in the abstract
Possible recall/reporting bias: people with headaches may be more attentive to and report other symptoms
Full text and covariate list not verified beyond the abstract; online ahead of print
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no competing interests; academic cohort study (Ahvaz Jundishapur University of Medical Sciences, with one Stanford-affiliated co-author). No manufacturer involvement or funding source disclosed in the record provided.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Periodontal Procedure Intensity and Incident Tinnitus in Korean Adults: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
items.whyMatters: In a very large Korean insurance database, people who needed more intensive gum-disease treatment were slightly more likely to be later diagnosed with tinnitus — a small association that may simply reflect more frequent doctor visits. It does not mean gum treatment causes tinnitus, and it does not point to any new tinnitus treatment.
items.summary: First nationwide claims-based cohort to use periodontal *procedure intensity* as a proxy for periodontal disease burden and link it to incident tinnitus, reporting a modest 24% higher adjusted hazard in the moderate-to-severe procedure group. It adds a new candidate risk-factor association to tinnitus epidemiology, not any treatment evidence. Incidence 4.38 vs 3.87 per 1000 person-years (moderate-to-severe vs mild); adjusted HR 1.24 (95% CI 1.17–1.30)

detail.population: Korean adults aged ≥40 with an ICD-10 K05 periodontal disease diagnosis who underwent periodontal treatment and had national health-screening data (NHIS-HEALS cohort, 2002–2019)
detail.primaryEndpoint: Incident tinnitus, defined as ICD-10 H93.1 recorded at ≥2 outpatient visits to neurology or otolaryngology
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Sex- and age-stratified analyses; sensitivity analyses using stricter tinnitus case definitions
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic or perceptual measurement of tinnitus was performed; the outcome is an administrative diagnosis code only.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no THI/TFI/TQ, anxiety, sleep or QoL instruments were used; this is an incidence study, not a symptom-severity study.
detail.otherOutcomes: Not reported — no audiometric, hearing, sleep, or oral-health-outcome data were available in the claims dataset
detail.safety: Not reported — the study did not assess adverse events of dental procedures; the authors explicitly note short-term procedure-related factors were unavailable, so the association cannot be read as procedural harm.
limitations: Exposure is an indirect surrogate (procedure intensity) rather than a direct clinical measure of periodontal disease severity
Claims-based outcome (ICD-10 H93.1) with no audiological confirmation, no loudness or severity measurement
Likely detection/surveillance bias: patients receiving more intensive dental care have more healthcare contact and more opportunity for a tinnitus code
No data on hearing loss, noise exposure, ototoxic medication or other key auditory confounders
No prespecified lag-time analysis, so reverse causation and short-term procedural effects cannot be excluded
Single-country (Korean) cohort restricted to adults ≥40 already diagnosed with periodontal disease, limiting generalizability
Observational design: no causal inference and no mechanistic (inflammatory) confirmation
detail.funding: independent — academic Korean authors (dental hygiene, physiology, paramedicine), authors declare no conflicts of interest; no manufacturer involvement and no funding source stated in the record provided
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Adolescent survey links heavy ultra-processed food intake with self-reported constant tinnitus
items.whyMatters: In a survey of 1,285 Belgrade teenagers, those reporting constant tinnitus were about 2.5 times more likely to fall in the highest ultra-processed food consumption group, alongside poorer sleep and lower school performance. Because everyone was surveyed at a single point in time, this cannot show that diet causes tinnitus — or that changing diet would help it.
items.summary: A large school-based cross-sectional survey in Belgrade reports that self-reported constant tinnitus is one of the strongest correlates of being in the highest tertile of a frequency-based proxy score for ultra-processed food (UPF) consumption among adolescents (aOR 2.55). The novelty is the pairing of a UPF dietary proxy with adolescent tinnitus, an association that has been little examined, but the design cannot establish direction or causality. Constant tinnitus aOR = 2.55 (95% CI 1.77-3.67); lower academic achievement aOR = 2.10 (1.38-3.21); alcohol consumption aOR = 1.34 (1.04-1.74); waking tired vs rested aOR = 1.58 (1.06-2.35); energy drink consumption frequency overall p < 0.001

detail.population: Secondary-school students aged 15-19 years from 12 four-year secondary schools in Belgrade, Serbia, sampled via stratified multistage cluster probability sampling
detail.primaryEndpoint: Membership in the highest tertile of a questionnaire-derived, frequency-based proxy UPF consumption score (binary outcome in logistic regression)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Associations of academic achievement, alcohol use, energy drink frequency, sleep-related items (waking tired vs rested), and self-reported constant tinnitus with the UPF proxy outcome
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic measurement of the tinnitus percept was performed; tinnitus was a self-reported binary/categorical item ('constant tinnitus') with no loudness matching or loudness rating.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no validated distress instrument (THI/TFI/TQ) or anxiety/depression outcome for tinnitus was reported; this is an association study, not a treatment study.
detail.otherOutcomes: Sleep-related self-report (waking tired vs rested), academic achievement, alcohol and energy drink consumption were associated with the highest UPF proxy category; no hearing measures, no audiometry, no quality-of-life instrument reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational survey with no intervention.
limitations: Cross-sectional design — temporal direction between diet and tinnitus cannot be established
Tinnitus ascertained by a single self-report questionnaire item, with no audiometry, no loudness matching and no validated distress measure
Outcome modeled is UPF consumption, not tinnitus, so the tinnitus association is a covariate finding rather than a pre-specified tinnitus hypothesis
The UPF score is an unvalidated frequency-based proxy built from seven food categories, with arbitrary empirical tertile cut-points
Single-city adolescent sample (Belgrade), limiting generalizability
Multiple comparisons across many lifestyle variables raise the risk of chance findings; residual confounding (e.g., noise exposure, headphone use, psychological distress) not addressed
Self-report throughout, with likely recall and social-desirability bias
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest; all affiliations are academic/public hospitals in Serbia; no manufacturer involvement. Funding source not stated in the available record.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Clinic study of 293 patients: measured tinnitus loudness barely tracks tinnitus distress
items.whyMatters: In nearly 300 patients, how loud the tinnitus measured in the clinic was had little relation to how much it bothered people; distress tracked better with depression, sound intolerance and how the sound was perceived. That supports the widespread clinical experience that reducing distress, not just the volume of the sound, is what matters for quality of life.
items.summary: A cross-sectional correlational study (N=293) in a single clinical setting reporting that tinnitus handicap (THI) is independently associated with subjective pitch, sound intolerance and depressive symptoms, while psychoacoustically matched tinnitus intensity was NOT associated with THI (and its correlation with subjective loudness did not survive Bonferroni correction). It adds another dataset reinforcing the known dissociation between measured loudness and distress. No effect sizes, correlation coefficients or p-values are given in the available abstract. Reported directionally: THI correlated positively with subjective loudness, pitch, complexity, sound intolerance, BDI and GAD-7; no significant association between THI and psychoacoustic tinnitus intensity; after Bonferroni correction, psychoacoustic intensity vs subjective loudness, psychoacoustic intensity vs THI-Functional, duration vs subjective loudness, subjective loudness vs BDI/GAD-7, and age vs subjective loudness/pitch were no longer significant.

detail.population: Adults with primary subjective tinnitus attending a single ENT/audiology clinic, evaluated otorhinolaryngologically and audiologically; no control group
detail.primaryEndpoint: Correlations between tinnitus characteristics (psychoacoustic intensity, subjective loudness, pitch, complexity, sound intolerance) and THI, BDI, GAD-7 scores
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Linear regression models of THI on sound intolerance, pitch and BDI; associations with tinnitus duration and age
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — this is an observational correlation study with no intervention; it measures how psychoacoustic loudness matching relates to other variables and notably finds matched tinnitus intensity unrelated to handicap, but it does not test or change loudness for any treatment.
detail.distressOutcome: none — no treatment was administered; the study only describes cross-sectional associations between distress (THI/BDI/GAD-7) and tinnitus features.
detail.otherOutcomes: Sound intolerance (hyperacusis-type) measured as a correlate and an independent predictor of THI; depression (BDI) and anxiety (GAD-7) symptom levels reported as correlates. No sleep or quality-of-life instruments reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — observational questionnaire and audiological assessment study with no intervention.
limitations: Cross-sectional design — no causal inference possible
Single centre, no control group, likely clinic-referral selection bias
No effect sizes, correlation coefficients or p-values available in the abstract record
Multiple comparisons: several associations lost significance after Bonferroni correction
Subjective loudness/pitch/complexity ratings are self-report and not standardised across sites
No longitudinal follow-up; no treatment outcomes
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest; affiliations include private clinics (Maihoub ENT Clinic, Opera Clinic/Protone Audio Kft.) but no manufacturer funding or device under evaluation is disclosed.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Uncontrolled Spanish cohort sorts 564 tinnitus patients into five phenotypes and reports distress improvement after four months of customised sound therapy
items.whyMatters: Researchers grouped patients into five 'types' of tinnitus and found that those who started out most distressed improved most on questionnaires after four months of daily customised sound. Because there was no comparison group and only patients who finished were counted, this cannot show that the sound therapy itself caused the improvement — and nothing here suggests the tinnitus sound got quieter.
items.summary: A retrospective Spanish cohort (n=564) applies data-driven clustering to derive five tinnitus phenotypes and then examines how each phenotype responded to four months of customised enriched acoustic environment (EAE) sound therapy. The novelty is the phenotype-stratified response analysis, not any new evidence that EAE works — the treatment arm is uncontrolled and analysed in completers only. Average tinnitus severity reduction of 24.3 points, described as clinically relevant and statistically significant, in 78% of subjects who completed the four-month treatment; larger absolute improvement in severity and emotional scores in phenotypes PH3 and PH4, but relative severity change notably smaller in PH4

detail.population: Retrospective cross-sectional cohort of adults with tinnitus attending a Spanish tinnitus service, characterised by audiogram pattern, demographics, tinnitus descriptors and emotional measures; a subset received EAE treatment
detail.sampleSize: 564 subjects clustered; number who actually started and completed the 4-month EAE treatment is not clearly stated in the abstract
detail.primaryEndpoint: Not reported — the clustering solution (five phenotypes) plus change in tinnitus severity score (scale not specified in the abstract; likely THI) after 4 months of EAE
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Change in emotional/distress scores by phenotype; composition of excluded, dropped-out and non-improved subjects across phenotypes
detail.comparisonType: within-group only — NEVER present within-group improvement as proof of efficacy
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no psychoacoustic loudness matching or loudness rating of the percept is reported; the 24.3-point change is a severity/handicap questionnaire outcome and says nothing about the loudness of the tinnitus itself.
detail.distressOutcome: limited — a large uncontrolled within-group drop in a distress/severity questionnaire among completers only, with no control arm, no randomisation, no blinding and unaccounted dropouts, so regression to the mean, natural history and expectancy cannot be separated from any treatment effect.
detail.otherOutcomes: Emotional symptom scores improved most in the phenotypes with the highest baseline distress; hearing-loss pattern was used as a classifying variable rather than an outcome. No sleep or quality-of-life outcomes reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — no adverse events, tolerability or dropout-for-harm data described in the abstract.
limitations: Retrospective, uncontrolled, no sham or comparison arm
Not randomised, not blinded
Completer-only analysis (78% figure applies to those who finished); excluded and dropped-out subjects not analysed as intention-to-treat
Severity instrument not named in the abstract; unclear whether THI, TFI or a local scale
Clusters derived and tested in the same dataset with no external validation cohort
Phenotype-by-response comparisons are exploratory and vulnerable to multiplicity
No loudness or psychoacoustic outcome at all
Authors' group has long developed and published on EAE — developer allegiance even though no financial COI is declared
detail.funding: independent — authors declare no conflicts of interest and affiliations are academic/public research (CSIC, Universidad Europea de Madrid, Ecole Centrale Méditerranée); however the senior group are the originators of the EAE approach, which is an allegiance bias worth noting even absent manufacturer funding.
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.

items.title: Large sham-controlled trial of ear vagus nerve stimulation plus notched music therapy registered in China (not yet recruiting)
items.whyMatters: Researchers plan a 444-person, sham-controlled trial to test whether adding transcutaneous ear vagus nerve stimulation to notched music therapy helps chronic tinnitus more than the music therapy alone. It is a well-designed plan with a one-year follow-up and measures of both tinnitus loudness and distress, but it has not started and no results are expected until around 2030.
items.summary: A new ClinicalTrials.gov registration (first posted 31 Aug 2026, not yet recruiting) for a planned multicenter, randomized, quadruple-blind, sham-controlled trial of taVNS added to tailor-made notched music therapy (TMNMT) in 444 adults with chronic subjective tinnitus, with 12-month follow-up and both loudness-matching and THI endpoints. No data exist — estimated start Oct 2026, primary completion Oct 2030.

detail.population: Adults 18-70 with chronic subjective tinnitus ≥6 months, tinnitus pitch 125-8000 Hz, hearing threshold ≤70 dB HL, THI ≥38; excludes conductive loss, Meniere's, pulsatile/vascular tinnitus, severe psychiatric disease, retrocochlear lesions
detail.primaryEndpoint: Responder rate at 3 months, defined as ≥7-point reduction in THI from baseline (a distress/handicap measure, not loudness)
detail.secondaryEndpoints: Responder rate at 6 and 12 months; change in VAS tinnitus loudness; change in audiometric tinnitus loudness match; BAI anxiety; BDI depression; PSQI sleep; resting-state EEG; MRI features; treatment-related adverse events. Exploratory: gut microbiome diversity, blood metabolomics and proteomics.
detail.loudnessOutcome: none — no results exist; the protocol does prespecify both VAS loudness and audiometric loudness matching as secondary outcomes, so if completed it could eventually inform the loudness question for taVNS+TMNMT, but nothing can be concluded now.
detail.distressOutcome: none — the primary endpoint is a THI responder rate (distress/handicap), but no data have been collected.
detail.otherOutcomes: Planned sleep (PSQI), anxiety (BAI), depression (BDI), EEG/MRI neuroimaging and microbiome/omics outcomes — all prospective, none reported.
detail.safety: Not reported — a safety outcome (auditory and non-auditory treatment-related adverse events, including ear/auricle burns, otalgia, hearing loss, tinnitus worsening, dizziness, headache, palpitations) is prespecified, and a DMC is in place, but no data are available.
limitations: Registration only — not yet recruiting, no participants, no data; primary completion estimated 2030

Stimulation parameters as listed are unusual/implausible for taVNS (0.1 Hz with 250-1000 ms pulse width, 0-0.5 mA); likely a registry data-entry error or non-standard protocol, and cannot be verified without a published protocol
Sham arm is described with the same parameters as the active arm ('initial sham stimulation parameters' identical), leaving the sham procedure and blinding integrity ambiguous
Add-on design (taVNS vs sham on top of TMNMT in both arms) tests only the incremental taVNS effect, not TMNMT itself
No blinding-integrity check or credibility assessment listed in the record
Single-country (China) multicenter trial; centers not yet listed; no published statistical analysis plan or power calculation in the record
detail.funding: independent — academic lead sponsor (Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital); no industry sponsor or collaborator listed; not FDA-regulated drug or device. Device manufacturer and funding source are not disclosed in the record.
detail.source: Sun Yat-Sen Memorial Hospital of Sun Yat-Sen University
detail.changesAssessment: No — this does not change our current evidence assessment.
